title: Changing how Google Photos estimates missing photo locations
text: Hi everyone, Google Photos can help you find, explore and look back on your photos and videos by their location, such as a city you visited on a recent trip. Your photos may have locations if you have your camera location settings turned on, or if you manually add a location. Previously, if some of your photos didn’t already have a location, Google Photos could estimate the location using information, such as visible landmarks in those photos and Location History , an opt-in Google account setting that saves where you go with your devices so you can enjoy personalized maps, recommendations and more. What’s changing: Google Photos has stopped using information from Location History to estimate locations for new photos and videos. Google Photos can still estimate locations using inputs such as visible landmarks and you’ll still be able to turn this “estimate missing locations” setting on or off in Photos at any time. Starting today, and rolling out gradually over the next few months, you may see a prompt when you open Google Photos that gives you the option to keep or delete your existing estimated locations. You’re in control: You will be able to choose to keep your existing estimated locations by signing into Google Photos and tapping “Keep” when prompted. If you don't choose to keep your estimated locations before May 1st, 2023, we will remove these estimations.  Rest assured, your photos will not be deleted. If you want to make changes to your location settings in Google Photos, you have the control to make edits and manage location sources at any time. If you want to change your camera location settings, you can adjust your preferences in your device settings. This change impacts your estimated locations in Google Photos and does not impact your Location History, which is a separate opt-in feature. Going forward, if you want to delete estimated locations from your photos, you can only do that in Google Photos. If you want to delete locations from your Location History, you may continue to do that within your Location History settings . Be on the lookout for the prompt to keep or delete your existing estimated locations. Thanks, Google Photos Team

title: New ways to find out if Photos are edited with AI
text: Hey everyone, We’re excited to share a helpful new section under the info panel called “How this was made.” This feature gives you a transparent look at a photo’s journey from its original capture to any edits applied along the way. With growing concerns around image authenticity, Google Photos have taken a big step forward to implement and support the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) standard. The “How this was made” section in the photo details is powered by C2PA metadata which means: You can now find the detailed information about how an image was created or edited. You can now trace whether it was generated, enhanced, or manipulated with AI tools. The data is securely embedded in the file and can be verified by anyone. With AI-generated images becoming more common, transparency is key. But it’s important to note that C2PA doesn’t determine if content is trustworthy. It simply shows you how your image was captured, created or edited. You’ll still need to apply your own judgement and media literacy skills to decide what to believe, especially when dealing with manipulated or AI-generated visuals. Learn how Content Credentials reveal helpful information that’s usually hidden . Let us know what you think, and as always, keep the feedback coming. Your input helps improve transparency tools and ensures AI-powered features work better for everyone. Learn how Google Photos helps you identify how photos were made . Thanks, Google Photos Team

title: Feature Request: Fix Boundary Detection and Add Manual Adjustments for Overlapping Pets
text: The Problem:  The automated grouping system hits a major technical bottleneck when tracking multiple animals. Currently, when two similarly colored cats or dogs are lying down, cuddling, or sitting close together, the system frequently misidentifies them as one single, large animal instead of two separate pets. Because the system draws a single bounding box around both animals, there is currently no way to separate them or correctly tag each individual pet in the photo. The Solution:  Improve the boundary detection for animals and give users control over the highlighted selections. This update should include: *Enhanced Edge Separation: Improve the AI's ability to differentiate separate animal shapes, even when pets share similar fur colors and are touching or overlapping. *Manual Boundary Adjustment: Give users the ability to manually adjust, resize, or split the highlighted selection boxes directly on the image when the AI miscalculates where one pet ends and another begins. This would allow users to draw two separate circles or boxes to correctly assign each pet their own face tag.

title: Feature Request: Duplicate photo & video detection and smart merging
text: ### Feature Request: Duplicate Photo & Video Detection and Smart Merging Google Photos should provide an option to **detect and merge duplicate or identical photos and videos** that are stored multiple times. Many users have the same photo or video saved in their storage more than once, which unnecessarily consumes storage space. The feature should work as follows: 1. **Automatically detect duplicates** Google Photos should scan the user's library and identify identical or highly similar photos and videos. 2. **Show duplicate groups** Users should be able to see all duplicate copies grouped together and review them before making any changes. 3. **Let the user choose which copy to keep** The user should have the option to select the photo/video they want to keep. 4. **Preserve the original/first-added date** When multiple copies of the same photo or video are merged, the system should keep the **date and time of the first time that photo/video was originally added to Google Photos**. 5. **Remove unnecessary duplicate copies** After the user confirms, all unwanted duplicate copies should be removed, while the selected copy remains safely stored. 6. **Preserve important information** The original date, location, albums, captions, and other relevant metadata should be preserved wherever possible. 7. **Storage-saving information** Google Photos should show the user how much storage space can be recovered by removing duplicates. ### Example If the same photo exists **5 times**, Google Photos should recognize that they are duplicates and show them as one group. The user can select the best copy to keep. After confirmation, the other 4 copies can be removed. The remaining photo should retain the **original date/time from when the photo was first added**, rather than changing to the date of the most recently uploaded copy. This feature would be extremely useful for users with large photo and video libraries because duplicate files can consume a significant amount of storage unnecessarily.
